triage.name: Wernicke encephalopathy
triage.reason: Acute confusional state with ophthalmoplegia and ataxia in a malnourished or alcohol-using patient; a high-yield interview and exam diagnosis.

demographics: More common in people with chronic heavy alcohol use
Also seen in anyone with prolonged poor nutrition or malabsorption

risk_factors.text: Poor nutrition or prolonged inadequate thiamine intake
Cancer with prolonged poor intake or chemotherapy

social_history: Unstable housing or poor access to food
Recent hospitalization or prolonged poor oral intake

chief_complaints.text: My vision is blurry and my eyes feel funny

hpi.onset: Subacute over days, sometimes hours; often noticed by family or staff rather than the patient
hpi.duration: Days to a couple of weeks at presentation
hpi.progression: Confusion and unsteadiness worsen over days; if untreated, drowsiness can progress to coma
hpi.location: Generalized; eye and balance symptoms are central
hpi.quality: Fluctuating confusion with poor balance and abnormal eye movements
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; can become life-threatening if untreated
hpi.timing: Continuous, often worse when trying to walk or read
pertinent_negatives: New medications that could cause confusion

argues_against: Painful red eye with vision loss
Prominent hallucinations or delusions without confusion

atypical.how_it_differs: Hyperemesis gravidarum with prolonged vomiting can cause thiamine deficiency; presentation may be attributed to pregnancy rather than encephalopathy.
Confusion may be mistaken for dementia or delirium from other causes; eye findings can be subtle.
Rare; can occur with malnutrition, prolonged vomiting, or inborn errors of metabolism; irritability and lethargy may dominate.
May present with nonspecific encephalopathy and be attributed to infection or medications.

general.mild: Awake but inattentive and disoriented to time or place; unsteady when standing
general.moderate: Confused and disoriented, needs help to walk, may be drowsy but rousable
general.severe: Markedly confused or stuporous, unable to stand or walk without support, abnormal eye movements obvious
general.critical: Obtunded to comatose, unresponsive or minimally responsive, at risk of aspiration and respiratory failure

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient their name, the date, and where they are
findings.finding: Disoriented to time and place, with fluctuating attention

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to repeat digits or count backward from 20
findings.finding: Difficulty sustaining attention, drifts off task

findings.maneuver: Ask about recent events and test recall of three words after a few minutes
findings.finding: Poor recent memory and difficulty learning new information

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to follow your finger to the right and left, then observe the eyes at rest
findings.finding: Horizontal nystagmus, often bilateral and more prominent on gaze to one side

findings.maneuver: Test extraocular movements in all directions and check for conjugate gaze
findings.finding: Weakness or palsy of one or more extraocular muscles, sometimes with impaired conjugate gaze

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to look to each side and observe whether the eye fails to abduct
findings.finding: Failure of one eye to abduct fully, causing horizontal diplopia

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to look to the right and left and observe conjugate movement
findings.finding: Impaired conjugate gaze to one or both sides

findings.maneuver: Observe the eyelids at rest and ask the patient to keep the eyes open
findings.finding: Drooping of one or both upper eyelids

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to walk a few steps and to stand with feet together
findings.finding: Wide-based unsteady gait, worse with eyes open, and difficulty with tandem walking

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to sit upright without support and observe the trunk
findings.finding: Swaying or inability to sit steadily without support

findings.maneuver: Perform the finger-to-nose test and the heel-to-shin test
findings.finding: Overshooting or wobbling at the end of the movement

findings.maneuver: Test the biceps, brachioradialis, knee, and ankle reflexes
findings.finding: Reduced deep tendon reflexes

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's speech and behavior during the interview
findings.finding: Disorganized thinking and difficulty following the conversation

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's level of alertness during the interview
findings.finding: Drowsy but rousable, drifts off when not stimulated

findings.maneuver: Apply a painful stimulus and observe the response
findings.finding: Unresponsive or minimally responsive to voice and pain

findings.maneuver: Test strength in the arms and legs and check for facial asymmetry
findings.finding: No focal weakness or facial droop

findings.maneuver: Check neck stiffness and perform the Brudzinski and Kernig maneuvers
findings.finding: No neck stiffness or meningeal signs

findings.maneuver: Examine the optic discs with an ophthalmoscope
findings.finding: No optic disc swelling

findings.maneuver: Measure the temperature and observe for rigors
findings.finding: No fever

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scalp and ask about recent head injury
findings.finding: No scalp laceration, bruising, or signs of head trauma

labs.caveat: Hyponatremia is common in chronic alcohol use and malnutrition and can itself cause confusion; it does not explain the eye movement findings.
Hypomagnesemia often accompanies thiamine deficiency and must be corrected for thiamine therapy to work.
Refeeding syndrome can drop phosphate sharply after feeding is started.
Low potassium and magnesium are common in poor intake and alcohol use and can worsen confusion and arrhythmia risk.
Hypoglycemia is a reversible cause of confusion and must be excluded before attributing findings to Wernicke encephalopathy; check glucose before giving glucose-containing fluids.
Low albumin reflects malnutrition and chronic liver disease; it supports the nutritional deficiency but is not diagnostic.
Elevated AST with an AST/ALT ratio above 2 suggests alcohol-related liver injury and supports the underlying cause.
Supports chronic heavy alcohol use but is nonspecific.
Macrocytosis is common in alcohol use and folate deficiency; it is a clue, not a diagnosis.
Thrombocytopenia from alcohol, liver disease or folate deficiency; relevant before lumbar puncture.
Folate deficiency often coexists with thiamine deficiency and can contribute to confusion and macrocytosis.
B12 deficiency is a treatable mimic of the cognitive and gait findings.
Elevated in hepatic encephalopathy, which can mimic the confusion; ammonia levels correlate poorly with severity.
Thyroid disease is a reversible cause of confusion and should be excluded.
CSF is usually normal in Wernicke encephalopathy; mild pleocytosis should prompt consideration of infection.
Mildly elevated protein is nonspecific; marked elevation suggests another process.
Scores of 8 or more indicate hazardous alcohol use and support the underlying cause.

findings.finding: Prolonged QTc from hypomagnesemia or hypokalemia
Sinus tachycardia from alcohol withdrawal or poor intake
Atrial fibrillation or other atrial arrhythmia related to alcohol use
Nonspecific ST-T changes from electrolyte abnormalities

imaging.study: MRI brain with and without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When the diagnosis is uncertain or another cause of encephalopathy is suspected

findings.text: Symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial thalami and periventricular regions
Symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity around the third ventricle and aqueduct
Mammillary body enhancement or T2 hyperintensity
T2 hyperintensity in the tectal plate and periaqueductal gray
Diffusion restriction in the medial thalami or mammillary bodies
Normal MRI (does not exclude the diagnosis)

imaging.preferred_when: Emergency setting to exclude hemorrhage, mass or stroke before MRI

findings.text: Usually normal or shows only nonspecific atrophy
Low attenuation in the medial thalami (rarely seen)

Assess sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, renal function and anion gap in a malnourished or alcohol-using patient
Hypomagnesemia is common and must be corrected for thiamine therapy to be effective
Low phosphate is common and can worsen with refeeding
Assess for infection, anemia, macrocytosis and thrombocytopenia
Assess liver enzymes, albumin and bilirubin for chronic liver disease and malnutrition
Quantify alcohol use and support the underlying cause
Exclude hemorrhage, mass or stroke in an acute confusional state
initial.only_if: focal findings, head trauma, or the history cannot be obtained

confirmatory.test: MRI brain with and without IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Shows the characteristic symmetric medial thalamic and periventricular changes when the clinical diagnosis is uncertain

supporting.why: Exclude a treatable vitamin deficiency that mimics the cognitive and gait findings
Folate deficiency often coexists and contributes to confusion and macrocytosis
Exclude thyroid disease as a reversible cause of encephalopathy
Consider hepatic encephalopathy when liver disease is present
supporting.only_if: known or suspected cirrhosis with confusion

supporting.why: Exclude meningitis or encephalitis when fever, meningismus or an immunocompromised state is present
Look for aspiration pneumonia in a drowsy patient
supporting.only_if: cough, fever, hypoxia or a concerning lung exam

not_indicated.why: Not routine when the presentation is typical and there is no fever or meningismus
Not routine without respiratory symptoms or findings
Not routine when the presentation is typical and there are no focal findings or trauma
Not needed unless there is epigastric pain

decision_points: Check glucose first; give thiamine before any glucose-containing fluids in a malnourished or alcohol-using patient
Do not wait for MRI or a thiamine level to start thiamine when the clinical picture fits
Correct magnesium and potassium alongside thiamine
If fever or meningismus is present, treat for CNS infection and perform lumbar puncture before attributing findings to Wernicke encephalopathy

criteria.name: Clinical diagnosis of Wernicke encephalopathy
criteria.summary: Diagnosis is clinical, based on the presence of two or more of: dietary deficiency, eye movement abnormalities (nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia), cerebellar dysfunction (ataxia), and altered mental status or mild memory impairment. It can be made with fewer features when thiamine deficiency is strongly suspected.
items: Dietary deficiency or risk factor such as chronic heavy alcohol use
Ocular signs such as nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia
Altered mental status or mild memory impairment

differential.name: Hepatic encephalopathy
differential.why_considered: Chronic heavy alcohol use with confusion and unsteady gait; both occur in patients with alcohol-related liver disease.
differential.trigger: Known or suspected cirrhosis with confusion and asterixis

history: Known cirrhosis or prior episodes of confusion after gastrointestinal bleeding or constipation
Confusion fluctuates and worsens after meals or bleeding
No diplopia or eye movement complaints
exam: Fetor hepaticus, jaundice, spider angiomata, ascites
labs: Normal glucose and electrolytes unless coexisting
imaging: MRI without the symmetric medial thalamic or periventricular T2 changes of Wernicke encephalopathy
Signs of cirrhosis on abdominal imaging

differential.name: Alcohol intoxication or withdrawal delirium
differential.why_considered: Confusion, unsteady gait and agitation in a patient with heavy alcohol use.
differential.trigger: Recent heavy drinking or last drink within days with tremor, sweating and autonomic hyperactivity

history: Last drink within hours to days
Tremor, sweating, agitation, prior withdrawal seizures
No diplopia or visual complaints
exam: No ophthalmoplegia; nystagmus may be present but ataxia is less prominent
Confusion improves as withdrawal is treated
labs: Elevated blood alcohol level or a clear withdrawal timeline
imaging: MRI normal or shows only atrophy
No mammillary body or medial thalamic changes

differential.name: Hypoglycemia
differential.why_considered: Acute confusion and unsteadiness in a malnourished or alcohol-using patient.
differential.trigger: Low bedside glucose or symptoms that resolve with glucose administration

history: Diabetes with insulin or sulfonylurea use
Prolonged fasting or heavy drinking without food
Symptoms improve rapidly after eating or glucose
labs: Resolution of symptoms after glucose correction

differential.name: Central nervous system infection (meningitis or encephalitis)
differential.why_considered: Fever, confusion and altered mental status can mimic Wernicke encephalopathy, especially in immunocompromised patients.
differential.trigger: Fever, neck stiffness, headache or immunocompromise

history: Fever, headache, neck stiffness
Recent infection or immunocompromised state
No clear nutritional deficiency
exam: Nuchal rigidity, positive Brudzinski or Kernig sign
labs: CSF pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose
imaging: MRI may show meningeal enhancement or temporal lobe changes in herpes encephalitis

differential.name: Stroke (basilar or thalamic)
differential.why_considered: Sudden confusion, eye movement abnormalities and ataxia can occur with brainstem or thalamic infarction.
differential.trigger: Sudden onset of focal neurologic deficits or eye movement abnormalities

history: Abrupt onset of symptoms
Vascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation
No nutritional deficiency history
exam: Focal weakness, sensory loss, or cranial nerve palsy
Gaze palsy or internuclear ophthalmoplegia may be present
imaging: CT or MRI shows acute infarction in the thalamus, midbrain or pons
Diffusion restriction in a vascular territory

differential.name: Multiple sclerosis
differential.why_considered: Young patient with diplopia, ataxia and eye movement abnormalities.

history: Prior episodes of numbness, weakness or vision loss
Symptoms separated in time and space
No heavy alcohol use or malnutrition
exam: Optic neuritis with decreased visual acuity and pain with eye movement
imaging: Periventricular, juxtacortical or infratentorial T2 lesions

differential.name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
differential.why_considered: Malnutrition with confusion, memory problems and gait ataxia.

history: Vegan diet, pernicious anemia, or gastric surgery
Paresthesias and numbness
No eye movement complaints
imaging: MRI may show subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

differential.name: Thyroid disease (hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism)
differential.why_considered: Confusion and gait unsteadiness can occur with thyroid dysfunction.

history: Weight change, cold or heat intolerance, palpitations
No diplopia or eye movement abnormalities
No heavy alcohol use
exam: Goiter, bradycardia or tachycardia, tremor, delayed relaxation of reflexes

severity.mild: Early, uncomplicated: mild confusion and disorientation, subtle nystagmus, and unsteady gait but able to walk with assistance; no drowsiness.
severity.moderate: Established: clear confusion and disorientation, obvious nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia, ataxia requiring support to walk, and difficulty with memory.
severity.severe: Advanced: marked confusion or stupor, prominent ophthalmoplegia, unable to stand or walk without help, and significant memory impairment.
severity.critical: Life-threatening: obtunded to comatose, unresponsive or minimally responsive, at risk of aspiration, respiratory failure, and death if untreated.

red_flags.finding: Decreased level of consciousness or coma
red_flags.meaning: Severe encephalopathy with risk of aspiration and respiratory failure; urgent thiamine and supportive care needed
Suggests central nervous system infection; perform lumbar puncture and treat empirically

red_flags.finding: Focal neurologic deficit or sudden onset

red_flags.meaning: Rapidly reversible cause of confusion; correct glucose immediately and give thiamine before glucose-containing fluids
Can worsen confusion and cause seizures or arrhythmias; correct carefully

complications.name: Korsakoff syndrome
clues: Persistent memory impairment after acute symptoms resolve

complications.name: Aspiration pneumonia
clues: Fever, hypoxia, or abnormal chest exam

special_populations.differences: Hyperemesis gravidarum with prolonged vomiting can cause thiamine deficiency; symptoms may be attributed to pregnancy, and treatment should not be delayed.
Confusion may be mistaken for dementia or delirium from other causes; eye findings can be subtle, and a lower threshold for thiamine treatment is warranted.
Rare; can occur with malnutrition, prolonged vomiting, or inborn errors of metabolism; irritability and lethargy may dominate, and the classic triad is often incomplete.
May present with nonspecific encephalopathy and be attributed to infection or medications; maintain a high index of suspicion for thiamine deficiency.

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink, and how often?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic heavy daily use, which is the most common risk factor for thiamine deficiency

key_questions.question: Have you been eating regularly? Have you lost weight or had trouble keeping food down?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged poor intake, weight loss, or persistent vomiting causing dietary thiamine deficiency

key_questions.question: When did the confusion and unsteadiness start, and are they getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Subacute onset over days with progression; helps separate from sudden vascular events

key_questions.question: Are you seeing double or having trouble with your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Diplopia, blurred vision, or eye movement complaints pointing to ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus

key_questions.question: Has anyone noticed your eyes moving on their own or not tracking together?
key_questions.looking_for: Nystagmus or impaired conjugate gaze noticed by family or staff

key_questions.question: Do you have trouble with your balance or walking?
key_questions.looking_for: Ataxia, especially wide-based gait that is worse with eyes open

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent vomiting, including from pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Persistent vomiting such as hyperemesis gravidarum as a cause of thiamine depletion

key_questions.question: Have you had weight loss surgery, bowel surgery, or a condition that causes poor absorption?
key_questions.looking_for: Bariatric surgery, malabsorption, or chronic gastrointestinal disease

key_questions.question: Have you been hospitalized recently or received intravenous fluids or glucose?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged IV glucose without thiamine, which can precipitate or worsen the condition

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including water pills, diabetes medicines, or seizure medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: Furosemide, metformin, phenytoin, isoniazid, or prednisone, which can contribute to thiamine deficiency

key_questions.question: Any fever, headache, neck stiffness, or recent infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Features suggesting CNS infection, which must be excluded before attributing findings to Wernicke encephalopathy

key_questions.question: Did the symptoms come on suddenly, and is there any weakness on one side or trouble speaking?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset or focal deficits suggesting stroke rather than a metabolic encephalopathy

key_questions.question: Have you had any head injury or a fall?
key_questions.looking_for: Trauma that could explain confusion or eye findings and requires imaging

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, and when did you last eat?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk of hypoglycemia as a rapidly reversible cause of confusion

key_questions.question: Any trouble with memory or learning new things, even before this episode?
key_questions.looking_for: Memory impairment that may reflect coexisting or evolving Korsakoff syndrome

key_questions.question: Any hallucinations, delusions, or thoughts of harming yourself?
key_questions.looking_for: Psychiatric features that might suggest another cause or coexisting withdrawal

reasoning_points: Recognizes the classic triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, and ataxia, but knows the full triad is often incomplete
Identifies a risk factor for thiamine deficiency such as chronic heavy alcohol use, malnutrition, persistent vomiting, or malabsorption
Notes that the diagnosis is clinical and treatment with thiamine should not be delayed for imaging or a thiamine level
Checks glucose first and gives thiamine before any glucose-containing fluids in a malnourished or alcohol-using patient
Corrects magnesium and potassium alongside thiamine because thiamine therapy is ineffective when magnesium is low
Excludes look-alikes such as hypoglycemia, hepatic encephalopathy, alcohol withdrawal, CNS infection, and stroke
Considers MRI showing symmetric medial thalamic and periventricular T2/FLAIR changes when the diagnosis is uncertain
Recognizes the risk of progression to Korsakoff syndrome with persistent memory impairment if untreated

easy: Middle-aged adult with chronic heavy alcohol use
Classic triad of confusion, nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia
Clear history of poor nutrition or recent binge with little food intake
medium: Patient with only one or two features of the triad, such as confusion and ataxia without obvious eye findings
Coexisting hyponatremia or hypomagnesemia that also causes confusion
Older adult whose confusion is initially attributed to dementia or delirium
Pregnant patient with hyperemesis gravidarum and prolonged vomiting
hard: Patient with cirrhosis and confusion where hepatic encephalopathy is the competing diagnosis
Immunocompromised patient with nonspecific encephalopathy and possible CNS infection
Sudden onset of eye movement abnormalities and ataxia mimicking a brainstem or thalamic stroke
Normal MRI despite a clinical picture consistent with Wernicke encephalopathy
Patient who develops symptoms after receiving intravenous glucose without thiamine
